questions.question: Why use TypeScript instead of JavaScript?
questions.title: Why Typescript
questions.direct_answer: TypeScript adds a static type system on top of JavaScript: types are checked at compile time, then erased — the runtime output is plain JS. The wins: errors surface at build time instead of production, editors get autocomplete/refactoring powered by the types, and types become self-documenting contracts. The cost: a build step, type-maintenance overhead, and a learning curve.

Mental Model

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    TS[TS source with types] --> T[tsc type-check]
    T -->|type errors| FAIL[build fails - bug caught]
    T -->|types OK| JS[plain JS emitted - types erased]
    JS --> RUN[runtime: zero type overhead]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Structural typing (the philosophy that makes TS feel like JS): TS is NOT nominal — types match by SHAPE, not name. An object with the right fields satisfies a type regardless of where it was declared or what it's called. Verified: a function accepting `{name: string}` accepts any object with a name, including ones with extra fields at the call boundary. This is duck typing, checked ahead of time — which is why TS is incrementally adoptable in JS codebases where nominal typing would require re-declaring everything.

The soundness trade-off (the depth marker): TS is deliberately unsound in places for ergonomics — type assertions (`as`), `any`, and non-null assertions (`!`) let you override the checker; some generics edge cases admit runtime type mismatches. The design goal is 'practically useful,' not 'provably correct' (that's the difference from languages like Haskell or Rust's type systems). This is why 'trust the types' is a discipline, not a guarantee: escape hatches exist and code review guards them.

The erasure boundary (the runtime reality): types, interfaces, and type-only imports vanish in output. What REMAINS runtime-visible: enums (compile to objects), class definitions (runtime constructs), and parameter properties. This is why you can't type-check at runtime — `typeof` tests values, not types — and why runtime validation (Zod, io-ts) exists for data crossing the trust boundary: the network doesn't run your compiler.
